paragraphs: The AW169 is the helicopter you see on hospital pads and offshore platforms: twin engine, retractable gear, a cabin door wide enough for a stretcher, and a fenestron-free tail rotor on a slim boom. The model keeps the sponsons that house the main gear, the sliding door track and the chin window, which are the details that stop it reading as a generic light twin.

The mesh is 153,605 polygons and 176,778 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps - 6 at 4096x4096 and one at 2048x2048. That is enough for an air ambulance or corporate livery to sit cleanly along the fuselage without stretching across the door frames.

A rigged build is on this page at $199 for when the rotors turn and the gear retracts. The static model at $149 covers medical services and offshore visualisation, corporate aviation marketing, film and television, and games. On sale since 2018.

The 2017 Model S is the one with the smooth nose. Tesla dropped the black nose cone that mimicked a grille and replaced it with a body-coloured panel, which changed the whole face of the car and dated every render made before it. This build is that facelift version, with the flush door handles, the panoramic glass roof and the wide rear haunch.

The mesh runs 164,495 polygons and 188,846 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps - 6 at 4096x4096 and one at 2048x2048. Efficient for a full car, which is what lets several of them fill a street scene.

This page carries the earlier 2015 front as well at $149, and rigged builds of both at $169. Take a rigged one when the wheels turn or the doors open; take the static model for stills, showroom renders and background traffic. On sale since 2017.

The nacelle is where a wind turbine stops being a sculpture and starts being a machine, and almost nobody ever sees inside one. A cutaway solves that: the main shaft, the gearbox, the generator, the yaw drive and the cooling equipment laid out in the order they actually sit, with the housing opened rather than removed so the scale of the enclosure is still readable.

It runs 462,736 polygons and 493,150 vertices in quads and tris. The UVs overlap, which is the right economy on machinery built from repeated castings and fasteners, and it keeps the asset manageable for something this dense.

At $149 and built to CheckMate specification, it is aimed at renewable energy presentation, engineering and technical marketing, education and training material, investor and trade show visualisation, and documentary work. On sale since 2026.

A steam turbine is rows of blades getting progressively longer as the steam expands, and that progression is invisible from outside the casing. The cross section is the whole argument of the model: split the casing, show the rotor with its blade stages, the diaphragms, the bearings and the steam path, and a machine that looks like a metal drum becomes something you can explain.

It runs 217,618 polygons and 238,154 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps at 8192x8192. That texture resolution is unusual and deliberate: on a cutaway the cut faces, the machined surfaces and the labelling carry the explanation, so they have to hold at magnification.
At $139 it suits power engineering presentation, technical education and training, industrial marketing, trade show and investor material, and documentary work. On sale since 2019.

The A350 is recognisable from the front before you can read the titles: the curved black mask around the flight deck windows and the upswept wingtips are unlike anything else in the sky. In Emirates colours it carries the red tail and the gold Arabic script along the fuselage, both of which have to follow the body curvature correctly to look painted rather than pasted.

The mesh is 320,971 polygons and 332,297 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 20 texture maps at 4096x4096. That budget covers the door outlines, the service stencils and the composite panel joints that a widebody shows along its flank.

A rigged build sits on this page at $149 for when the gear and control surfaces move. The static model at $129 covers airline marketing, airport and terminal visualisation, film and television, news graphics and print. On sale since 2017.

This is the assembled phone with everything inside it modelled: the logic board, the battery, the camera module, the taptic engine and the shields sitting in their real positions behind a closed chassis. That combination is what a cutaway needs - the device has to look like a finished product until the moment the housing goes transparent and the interior is revealed.

It runs 262,865 polygons and 280,925 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 56 texture maps at 4096x4096. That count exists because every internal board and shield carries its own printed detail, and printed detail is exactly what makes an internal shot convincing rather than decorative.
At $99 it is aimed at product and technology advertising, engineering and design presentation, technology journalism, teaching material and repair documentation. On sale since 2021.

A kiwi carries almost all of its character in two places: the long probing bill with nostrils right at the tip, and the low crouched stance that comes from having no useful wings and legs set far back. This build keeps the shaggy hair-like plumage that covers the body and the heavy three-toed feet that do the digging.

The mesh is 149,887 polygons and 294,577 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. The vertex count running well above the polygon count is what a soft rounded animal needs - it keeps the back and crown smooth where a coarser cage would show facets in silhouette.

Three rigged builds share this page: a general one at $139 and versions prepared for Cinema 4D and for Maya at $99 each. Take a rigged one for animation; the static model at $99 covers wildlife documentary, conservation material, education, tourism and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2023.

An octopus is the hardest kind of animal to model because it has no fixed shape. The mantle changes volume, the arms taper over their whole length and curl in every direction, and the suckers have to run in a double row that thins toward the tip. This build handles all three, which is what lets it read as a soft-bodied animal rather than a rubber toy.

The mesh is 60,158 polygons and 60,136 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 6 texture maps at 4096x4096. The texture work is doing heavy lifting here: skin mottling, the sheen of a wet surface and the darker sucker rims are what sell the creature at close range.

At $99 and built to StemCell specification, it suits marine documentary and education, aquarium and museum material, seafood and restaurant advertising, film and television, and games. On sale since 2017.

A tactical uniform is a system rather than a garment: base layers, a plate carrier over them, pouches on the carrier, a belt rig, knee protection and the straps that hold it all together. The layering is what makes it read correctly, because the bulk sits in specific places and a smooth suit with pockets painted on fools nobody.

The mesh is economical at 32,574 polygons and 33,487 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. That weight is deliberate: uniforms are usually needed several at a time, and a team of six should not cost more than the scene they are standing in.

At $79 and built to CheckMate specification, it is aimed at law enforcement and defence visualisation, film and television costume reference, games, training material and equipment presentation. Real-world scale is kept, so it fits a standard human figure without rescaling.

Security screening is the part of an airport everyone recognises and almost nobody models properly. A checkpoint needs more than one machine type - the walk-through arch, the millimetre wave booth with its curved panels, the operator screen - and they have to sit in a sensible order for the flow to make sense. This is a collection rather than a single scanner, which is what a believable checkpoint actually requires.

Having several units in one purchase means a terminal can be dressed with a full lane rather than the same machine repeated, and a queue can be staged around equipment that behaves like real hardware.

A second collection sits on this page at $99 for a wider selection. This set at $69 is built to CheckMate specification and aimed at airport and terminal visualisation, security industry presentation, film and television, training material and games. On sale since 2021.

The Augustus portrait type is one of the most reproduced faces in history, and it is a piece of political design as much as a likeness: the calm expression, the distinctive comma-shaped fringe over the forehead, and a face that never ages across decades of statues. This bust keeps that hairline and the set of the jaw, which are what make the emperor recognisable rather than merely Roman.

The mesh is 19,038 polygons and 10,134 vertices in quads and tris. The UVs overlap, which is the sensible economy on a symmetrical marble subject where a mirrored layout costs nothing visible, and the StemCell build means it works in a real-time engine.
At $59 it suits museum and exhibition work, classical education material, interior and set dressing, historical documentary, games and print. On sale since 2023.

The missile used by NASAMS is an air-to-air weapon adapted to launch from the ground, which is the whole reason the system exists and the reason the missile looks the way it does: slender body, cruciform forward fins, larger tail fins and a seeker dome at the nose. This model keeps the fin geometry and the umbilical and lug detail along the body.

It is deliberately light at 12,106 polygons and 6,601 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and built to StemCell specification. That weight matters, because a missile is almost never needed alone - a launcher holds several, and a scene may need a salvo in flight.

At $59 it is aimed at defence visualisation, news and documentary graphics, military training material, games and print. Real-world scale is kept, so it seats correctly in a launcher canister. On sale since 2023.

A dry bag is defined by how it closes: the top is rolled down several turns and clipped, which leaves a stiff folded lip and gives the bag its distinctive tapered shape. Modelled worn on a back, it also has to show where the straps compress it and where it sits against the body, because a dry bag hanging perfectly cylindrical looks like a barrel.

The mesh is 28,236 polygons and 28,085 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout. That is a sensible budget for a coated fabric object whose interest lies in the roll-top fold, the seam welds and the strap hardware.

At $49 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits outdoor and adventure sports visualisation, kayaking and rafting material, travel and equipment advertising, character set dressing and games. On sale since 2026.

Starting boxes are a piece of track furniture with a very specific job: hold eight dogs still, then open every door at exactly the same instant. That requirement shapes the object - a long steel frame, numbered coloured doors, a shared release mechanism along the top and a rear loading gate for each stall. The numbering and the colour order are part of the sport, and they are modelled here rather than left to a texture.
The mesh is 173,412 polygons and 89,302 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the detail concentrated in the frame, the mesh doors and the release gear.
At $49 it suits sports broadcast graphics, racing venue visualisation, betting and gaming applications, film and television, and animal sport documentary. On sale since 2022.
